title: The Supervisor / Worker Pattern
summary: In the supervisor/worker pattern one agent owns the goal: it decomposes the task into subtasks, routes each to a specialist worker, and integrates the results into a final answer. The supervisor holds the plan and the shared context; workers stay narrow, stateless, and replaceable — which is what makes the whole system controllable.

subtopics.title: The supervisor owns the goal and the plan
subtopics.explanation: The supervisor is the only agent that sees the whole task; it decides what needs doing, in what order, and who does it, then assembles the pieces. Workers never talk to each other — all coordination flows through the supervisor, which keeps control centralised and traceable. Concentrating the plan in one place is what makes a supervisor/worker system debuggable instead of a free-for-all.

subtopics.title: Decompose the task into subtasks
subtopics.explanation: Decomposition is the supervisor asking the model to break the goal into a small set of self-contained subtasks, each expressible as an instruction plus the worker best suited to it. Good subtasks are independent enough to route separately and have a clear 'done' condition. Getting decomposition right is the highest-leverage step: a clean split makes routing and integration trivial, while a muddy one poisons everything downstream.
subtopics.example:
def decompose(self, goal):
    # ask the model for a structured plan (validated elsewhere)
    return [
        Step(id="facts", worker="researcher",
             instruction=f"Gather key facts for: {goal}"),
        Step(id="draft", worker="writer",
             instruction="Write a summary using {facts}"),
        Step(id="check", worker="reviewer",
             instruction="Verify claims in {draft} against {facts}"),
    ]
# each step names ONE worker and one clear job

subtopics.title: Route each subtask to the right worker
subtopics.explanation: Routing maps a subtask to the specialist that can handle it — a researcher with search tools, a coder with a sandbox, a reviewer with none. The supervisor passes only the context that worker needs, keeping each worker narrow and its prompt small. Precise routing is what lets workers stay simple and stateless, which in turn makes them easy to test and swap.
subtopics.example:
def dispatch(self, step):
    worker = self.workers[step.worker]     # pick the specialist
    # fill the instruction with results this step depends on
    ctx = step.instruction.format(**self.results)
    return worker.run(ctx)                 # worker sees only its slice

# researcher never sees the reviewer's tools, and vice versa
# -> smaller prompts, clearer responsibilities

subtopics.title: Integrate the worker results
subtopics.explanation: Once subtasks return, the supervisor combines them — concatenating, reconciling, or feeding them to a final model call — into the single answer the caller asked for. Integration is also where the supervisor resolves conflicts between workers and drops or flags low-quality pieces. This merge step is the payoff of decomposition: it turns scattered specialist outputs back into one coherent result.
subtopics.example:
def integrate(self, goal, results):
    # final model call that fuses the pieces into one answer
    prompt = (
        f"Goal: {goal}\n"
        f"Facts: {results['facts']}\n"
        f"Draft: {results['draft']}\n"
        f"Review notes: {results['check']}\n"
        "Produce the final, corrected summary."
    )
    return llm(prompt)     # one coherent output, not three fragments

subtopics.title: Iterate and re-plan when a worker fails
subtopics.explanation: A rigid one-pass plan breaks the moment a worker returns something wrong or incomplete, so a robust supervisor inspects results and can re-dispatch, add a step, or re-plan. Bounding this with a max-iteration cap prevents runaway loops. Treating the plan as revisable rather than fixed is what upgrades the pattern from a brittle pipeline into an adaptive system.

foundations.overview: The supervisor/worker (also called orchestrator/worker) pattern gives one agent — the supervisor — sole ownership of the goal. It decomposes the task into a small set of self-contained subtasks, routes each to the specialist worker best equipped for it, and integrates the returned pieces into a single answer. Workers are deliberately narrow: they see only the slice of context they need, use only their own tools, and never talk to each other, so all coordination is centralised in the supervisor. This hub-and-spoke shape is what makes multi-agent tractable — the plan lives in one place, control is traceable, and workers stay stateless and replaceable. A production supervisor also treats its plan as revisable: it reviews worker output, re-dispatches or re-plans on failure, and bounds the whole thing with an iteration cap so it can adapt without looping forever.
foundations.formalDefinition: The supervisor/worker pattern is a multi-agent topology in which a single supervisor agent decomposes a goal into subtasks, dispatches each to a specialist worker agent (passing only the required context), collects the results, and integrates them into a final output, optionally re-planning based on a review of intermediate results, bounded by an iteration limit.
foundations.whyItMatters: It is the default way to add specialisation and (optionally) parallelism to an agent system without descending into chaos. Centralising the plan in one supervisor keeps a growing set of workers debuggable, testable, and safe — the alternative, agents freely messaging each other, is far harder to reason about and control.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a project manager and a team of contractors. The PM (supervisor) breaks the project into work orders, hands each to the right contractor (worker), and reviews and assembles what comes back; contractors don't coordinate among themselves and only see their own assignment. If a deliverable is wrong, the PM reissues that one work order.
foundations.whenToUse: Reach for it when a goal cleanly decomposes into subtasks with distinct skills or tools, when you want to run independent subtasks in parallel, or when you need one place to enforce policy and integrate results. Avoid it when subtasks are tightly coupled and constantly need each other's in-progress state — that is better as a single agent.
foundations.tradeoffs: You gain specialisation, parallelism, and a single control point for planning, safety, and integration. You pay coordination cost (context re-sent to each worker), added latency on sequential steps, and the risk that a poor decomposition or supervisor error propagates to every worker.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Research assistants that fan a question out to parallel search workers and synthesise, coding agents where a planner routes files to specialist editors and a test-runner, and document pipelines where a supervisor assigns chunks to summariser workers then merges the summaries.
commonUseCases: Fan-out research: parallel search workers, one synthesiser
Planner routing subtasks to specialist coders + a reviewer
Map-reduce over document chunks with a merge step
A single control point for policy, tool permissions, and integration

commonMisconceptions.myth: Workers should coordinate with each other to be efficient.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Peer-to-peer worker chatter destroys traceability. All coordination flows through the supervisor; workers stay narrow, stateless, and unaware of each other.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The supervisor just splits work once and is done.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A robust supervisor reviews results and can re-dispatch or re-plan on failure, bounded by an iteration cap — the plan is revisable, not fixed.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every worker needs the full context to do well.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Passing only the required slice keeps worker prompts small, cheaper, and more focused; over-sharing context raises cost and invites distraction.

checkpoints.prompt: In the supervisor/worker pattern, how do workers coordinate with each other?
options: They message each other directly to share state
They don't — all coordination flows through the supervisor
They share one global memory that all can edit
Each worker calls the next worker when it finishes
checkpoints.explanation: Coordination is centralised: workers are narrow and stateless and never talk to each other. The supervisor owns the plan, routes context, and integrates results, which is what keeps the system traceable and debuggable.

checkpoints.prompt: Given the re-planning supervisor, how many times does the worker run?
checkpoints.code:
# reviewer passes only if 'budget' appears
# worker: attempt 1 omits budget, attempt 2 includes it
out = supervisor("Draft a hiring plan", worker, reviewer, max_rounds=3)
print(worker.calls)
checkpoints.explanation: The first result fails review (no 'budget'), so the supervisor re-dispatches with the gap; the second result passes and the loop returns early. That is two worker calls, well under the max_rounds cap of 3.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the dispatch so the worker receives only the context its subtask depends on.
checkpoints.explanation: Filling the instruction template with **self.results injects exactly the prior subtask outputs this step depends on, keeping the worker's context to its own slice rather than the entire task state.

theory.question: Explain the supervisor/worker pattern and why coordination is centralised in the supervisor.
theory.directAnswer: One supervisor agent owns the goal: it decomposes the task into subtasks, routes each to a specialist worker with only the context that worker needs, and integrates the results into a final answer. Coordination is centralised because workers that message each other directly become untraceable and hard to control — routing everything through the supervisor keeps the plan in one place, workers narrow and stateless, and the whole system debuggable.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A hub-and-spoke multi-agent topology where a supervisor decomposes, routes, integrates, and optionally re-plans, while workers are narrow specialists that never talk to each other.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It adds specialisation and optional parallelism to an agent system without the chaos of peer-to-peer agents, giving a single point for planning, policy, tool-permission control, and result integration.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The supervisor asks the model for a structured plan of subtasks, dispatches each to the matching worker passing only its required slice of context, collects results, reviews them, re-dispatches or re-plans on gaps up to an iteration cap, and finally fuses the pieces into one answer.

theory.whyImportant: It is the default, most controllable way to scale beyond a single agent; understanding it lets you add capacity and specialisation while keeping the system testable and safe.
theory.realWorldExample: A research assistant supervisor fans a question out to several parallel search workers, reviews their findings for gaps, dispatches follow-up searches, then synthesises everything into one cited answer.

followUps.question: How do you keep worker prompts small?
followUps.answer: Route only the context each subtask depends on rather than the full task state; smaller prompts are cheaper, faster, and less prone to distraction.

followUps.question: What makes it adaptive rather than a brittle pipeline?
followUps.answer: The supervisor reviews results and can re-dispatch or re-plan on failure, bounded by an iteration cap, so a bad worker output is corrected instead of propagated.

theory.question: What are the main trade-offs of supervisor/worker versus a single agent?
theory.directAnswer: You gain specialisation, optional parallelism over independent subtasks, and a single control point for planning, safety, and integration. You pay coordination cost — context re-sent to each worker, added latency on sequential hops — and you take on the risk that a poor decomposition or a supervisor error propagates to every worker downstream.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A comparison between a centralised multi-agent topology and one well-tooled agent loop for the same task.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Splitting work lets specialists use distinct tools and lets independent subtasks run in parallel, but it introduces the overhead and failure modes any distributed system has.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The supervisor spends extra tokens re-sharing context per worker and extra wall-clock time on sequential steps; benefits appear only when subtasks are genuinely separable or parallelisable, so the split earns back its coordination tax.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the topology on evidence rather than instinct avoids the common trap of over-engineering a task a single agent handles more cheaply and reliably.
theory.realWorldExample: A team split a summarisation task into planner/writer/editor agents and saw cost triple with no quality gain, then collapsed it back to one agent — the subtasks were too coupled to justify the coordination cost.

followUps.question: When does the pattern actually reduce latency?
followUps.answer: Only when independent subtasks run in parallel; sequential handoffs add latency because each hop is another round-trip plus re-sent context.

followUps.question: How do you limit blast radius from a bad decomposition?
followUps.answer: Validate the plan before dispatch, keep subtasks small with clear done-conditions, and have the supervisor review results so a bad split is caught before integration.

scenario.question: You must build an agent that answers deep research questions by searching many sources. Would you use supervisor/worker, and how would you structure it?
scenario.directAnswer: Yes — this is a strong fit because the work is separable and parallelisable. Use a supervisor that decomposes the question into sub-questions, fans them out to parallel search workers (each with only its sub-question and search tools), reviews the collected findings for gaps and dispatches follow-up searches, then integrates everything into one cited synthesis, all bounded by a round cap.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A fan-out/fan-in supervisor/worker design where independent search subtasks run in parallel and a supervisor plans, reviews, and synthesises.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Research decomposes naturally into independent lookups, so parallel workers cut latency and a central supervisor is the clean place to plan sub-questions, dedupe, resolve conflicts, and produce citations.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The supervisor generates sub-questions, dispatches each to a stateless search worker in parallel, gathers results, self-reviews coverage and contradictions, issues targeted follow-ups for gaps, and finally calls a synthesis step that fuses findings with sources.

scenario.whyImportant: It demonstrates matching topology to the task: parallel separable subtasks are exactly where multi-agent earns its coordination cost, and centralising synthesis keeps citations and conflict-resolution coherent.
scenario.realWorldExample: A research agent split 'compare three databases for our workload' into per-database and per-criterion sub-questions, ran them in parallel, spotted a missing benchmark during review, dispatched one more search, and synthesised a single comparison table with sources.

followUps.question: How do you stop the supervisor from looping forever?
followUps.answer: Bound re-planning with a max-rounds cap and a token/time budget, and treat exhausting them as a routed 'best-effort answer with noted gaps' rather than an error.

followUps.question: How do workers avoid redundant searches?
followUps.answer: The supervisor decomposes into disjoint sub-questions and dedupes results on fan-in; workers stay unaware of each other, so dedup and conflict-resolution live in the supervisor.

keyTakeaways: The supervisor owns the goal: it decomposes the task, routes subtasks to specialist workers, and integrates the results.
Workers are narrow, stateless, and never talk to each other — all coordination flows through the supervisor for traceability.
Route only the context a subtask depends on, keeping worker prompts small, cheaper, and more focused.
A robust supervisor reviews results and re-dispatches or re-plans on failure, bounded by an iteration cap.
Use it for separable or parallelisable subtasks; the cost is re-sent context and latency, so don't split tightly-coupled work.
